analysis.title: The AI Boom's Dirty Little Secret
key_insights: SocGen's Albert Edwards argues the market is overlooking liquidity in the latest AI sell-off. Excess liquidity has deteriorated sharply and has historically led equities, though the relationship is imperfect.

Breadth of analyst earnings revisions has started to deteriorate, particularly in tech, and the change in the pace of upgrades has rolled over. Earnings can keep growing while equities struggle if upgrade momentum fades (second-derivative problem).

Per Bloomberg's Simon White, semiconductors are the sector most positively sensitive to the yield curve, so further curve flattening on top of tighter liquidity could pressure semis. NVDA earnings and capex guidance are the focus, but the bond market may matter more.
Jefferies' Chris Wood sees the AI capex boom ending when credit markets stop funding it, not when demand disappears. AI-related credit spreads rose sharply, though some stress has eased recently.

Goldman estimates global AI-related debt issuance reached $687bn through November 3, with only 43% from the hyperscalers. The five biggest hyperscalers have issued $296bn this year, above Goldman's prior full-year forecast of $250bn.

BofA says off-balance-sheet AI commitments rose more than 50% between quarters. Including Nvidia's newly disclosed obligations, the combined total approaches $3.5 trillion. Not all of it is debt and some can be cancelled.

Goldman estimates hyperscalers need about $350bn of annual AI revenue to cover depreciation and operating costs of 2026-27 investments. Adding a return on capital raises the hurdle, and in one scenario the application layer needs more than $1tn of annual revenue.

GS tech specialist Jim Callahan questions the AI ecosystem's dependence on Jensen Huang. Nvidia has supported neoclouds through investments, commercial commitments and supplier relationships, and a new CEO may be less willing to use the balance sheet that way. Near-term chip demand may not change, but the longer-term financing model could.

Jefferies estimates AI-related investment contributed 1.39 percentage points of the 2.1% US real GDP growth over the year to Q3, roughly two-thirds of the increase. Information processing equipment and software investment is 5.35% of GDP, above the dot-com peak of 4.46%.

SocGen's Edwards notes year-on-year core inflation looks benign but shorter-term measures are rising again, and corporate output-price inflation remains above 4%. Another inflation surprise could leave the Fed facing sticky prices and weak equities at once.

Goldman cautions the AI capex boom is not over: hyperscalers retain financial firepower, cloud revenue backlogs are $1.8tn, and investment-grade credit can absorb another $500bn of issuance. The vulnerable part of the trade is the highly leveraged players rather than the cash-rich giants.
